As is the case with other complex pathologic conditions, 
pediatric cerebral aneurysms are best addressed at high-volume 
centers with dedicated, comprehensive neurovascular teams. 
A comprehensive team evaluates all pediatric patients with 
aneurysms at our institutions. Team members include those with 
expertise in microsurgery and endovascular techniques. Given 
that the life expectancy of pediatric patients with aneurysms is 
measured in decades, we have an institutional bias of treating 
pediatric aneurysms with microsurgery (when possible) because 
of its demonstrated durability.
The discussion that follows is based on the experience of the 
senior author (R.F.S.) in treating more than 6300 aneurysms 
over the past 30 years. The goals of aneurysm treatment include 
obliterating the lesion while preserving the parent vessel when 
possible.
Approaches to Pediatric Aneurysms
Treatment of pediatric aneurysms depends on patient presenta­
tion, location of the aneurysm, and the goals of care (Fig. 248.1). 
Successful aneurysm surgery depends on unhindered access to the 
site of pathology and inflow and outflow vessels.

aneurysms are twice as likely to occur in the posterior circulation. 
Giant aneurysms are also more common in the pediatric 
population. Common presenting symptoms include headaches, 
seizures, loss of consciousness, and motor/cranial nerve deficits.
Pediatric patients with aneurysms, much like their adult 
counterparts, can be treated with one or a combination of the 
following options: conservative follow-up, direct clipping, clip 
reconstruction, coil embolization of the aneurysm, endovascular 
flow diversion, surgical or endovascular hunterian ligation, 
wrapping, excision, and trapping with revascularization.
With improvements in surgical technique, the majority 
of aneurysms can now be directly clipped. An intraoperative 
evaluation of the aneurysm can shed light on the morphology 
of the aneurysm, the caliber and health of the parent vessel, 
the number and location of perforators, and skull base anatomy 
restricting access to the aneurysm neck. Adjuncts, such as 
hypothermic circulatory arrest, can simplify the treatment of 
complex lesions, notably those involving the basilar apex.
Excision alone is rarely possible or indicated in pediatric 
patients. The disease process leading to aneurysm formation may 
involve adjacent segments of the parent vessel, and care should be 
taken to minimize manipulation of friable tissues.

CHAPTER 248  Pediatric Cerebral Aneurysms
Several reports have highlighted the use of endovascular 
techniques for the treatment of pediatric aneurysms. Stiefel and 
coworkers67 reported on the use of endovascular and surgical 
techniques to treat 13 ruptured pediatric cerebral aneurysms. They 
reported that in a small subset of cases in which MRA follow-up 
was available (mean follow-up, 6 years), outcomes in patients 
treated with endovascular techniques and microsurgery were 
comparable. In another endovascular series from the University 
of California, Los Angeles, the investigators reported a 2.9% rate 
of permanent complications and a favorable outcome in 87% of 
cases.68 They noted two recurrences in 31 patients and no cases of 
de novo aneurysm formation during the follow-up period of 25.9 
months. Unfortunately, this series had follow-up angiograms in 
only 51% of cases, and follow-up was too short to draw definitive 
conclusions.68 In another series, 25 pediatric patients were treated 
between 1998 and 2005 with coil embolization or parent vessel 
occlusion, and 96% had a Glasgow Outcome Scale score of 4 or 
5 at 23.5 months of follow-up.69 Saraf and colleagues70 reviewed 
their experience treating 23 pediatric patients with endovascular 
techniques. At a mean follow-up of 3 years, they noted stable 
occlusion in 96% of patients. There were no deaths in this series, 
and only four patients had complications, which were permanent 
in only one patient.

is therefore mandatory.

coil embolization of the aneurysm with or without a stent as an 
adjunct, flow diversion or another endovascular reconstructive 
strategy, surgical or endovascular hunterian ligation, wrapping, 
excision, and trapping with revascularization.

Cerebral aneurysms in the pediatric population are rare. Most 
academic centers treat only one to two patients with these lesions 
per year. Since the early treatment of pediatric aneurysms, major 
advances have improved outcomes in children with these rare 
and challenging pathologic conditions. The full chapter, avail­
able at  ExpertConsult.com, provides details on the pathophysi­
ology, natural history, and types of these aneurysms (Video 
248.1). Detailed treatment options, including microsurgery and 
endovascular techniques, are described along with follow-up 
recommendations.
Aneurysms are exceedingly rare in the pediatric population, 
with a suggested prevalence rate of only 0.5% to 4.6%. Multiple 
aneurysms are less frequently observed in children than in adults.
The exact etiology of pediatric aneurysms is not known and is 
a controversial matter. Children are rarely exposed to the factors 
thought to cause aneurysm formation in adults (i.e., chronic stress 
caused by hypertension and inflammation). Because of this lack 
of exposure in children, some investigators have postulated that 
pediatric aneurysms are congenital; however, a large autopsy 
series in children did not detect any incidental aneurysms, casting 
doubt on a congenital etiology.

Judicious follow-up is a 
must, given the higher rates of recurrence and de novo aneurysm 
formation in the pediatric population. 
CONCLUSION
Pediatric cerebral aneurysms are exceedingly rare lesions. 
Accumulating evidence suggests that these aneurysms have 
aggressive natural histories, requiring immediate and aggres­
sive treatment. Although both microsurgery and endovascular 
techniques have documented good outcomes, microsurgery has 
demonstrated more durable long-term outcomes. Therefore at 
our institutions it is the recommended treatment of choice when 
possible. Regardless of the treatment method, pediatric cerebral 
aneurysms have a higher rate of recurrence and de novo aneu­
rysm formation than their adult counterparts, so long-term vas­
cular surveillance is mandatory.

Cerebral aneurysms in the pediatric population are rare, with 
most academic centers treating only one to two patients with 
these lesions per year.1 The first report of a pediatric cerebral 
aneurysm was by Eppinger2 in 1871. He consulted on a 15-year-
old boy who collapsed during physical exercise and died 3 days 
later. Postmortem studies revealed subarachnoid blood and an 
aneurysm arising from the anterior cerebral artery (ACA). Using 
this case as an anecdote, Eppinger3 suggested that ruptured 
aneurysms were the cause of cerebral hemorrhage of unknown 
etiology in children. In 1939 McDonald and Korb4 published 
a postmortem report on 61 children, raising awareness of rup­
tured aneurysms as a cause of sudden death in children. The 
first successful surgical repair and excision of a ruptured cerebral 
aneurysm was reported in 1960.5 Since this initial report, major 
advances have improved outcomes in children with these rare 
and challenging pathologic conditions. This chapter provides 
details on the pathophysiology, natural history, and types of these 
aneurysms (Video 248.1). Detailed treatment options, including 
microsurgery and endovascular techniques, are described along 
with follow-up recommendations.

FOLLOW-UP IMAGING RECOMMENDATIONS
In a Finnish study with excellent long-term follow-up (median 
34 years), the earliest symptomatic recurrent aneurysm (mani­
festing as epileptic seizures) was found 6 years after the patient’s 
initial treatment, and the first de novo aneurysm (manifesting as 
SAH) was at 11 years32; these results underscore the importance 
of close follow-up. Unfortunately, there is no routine agreed-on 
mode of follow-up for pediatric aneurysms.85 We recommend 
noninvasive imaging using MRA every 6 months for the first 24 
months after endovascular embolization and yearly for the first 3 
to 5 years after microsurgery. If the noninvasive imaging raises a 
concern, formal invasive angiographic studies should be consid­
ered. Thereafter we recommend vascular imaging every 3 to 5 
years for the duration of the patient’s life. Judicious follow-up is a 
must, given the higher rates of recurrence and de novo aneurysm 
formation in the pediatric population. 
CONCLUSION
Pediatric cerebral aneurysms are exceedingly rare lesions.

SECTION 8  Pediatrics
The ideal treatment option for pediatric aneurysms is a matter 
of debate. A study of national trends in patient management and 
treatment in the pediatric population revealed a 50% increase 
in the use of endovascular techniques between 2006 and 2009.43 
The same study noted a 50% increase in the cost of endovascular 
therapy and a 6% rise in the cost of surgical therapy between 
2000 and 2009; there was no change in the frequency of surgical 
therapy. Table 248.3 highlights some of the larger series 
describing surgical and endovascular treatment outcomes for 
pediatric patients with aneurysms.22-24
Conservative Management
Frequently, parents are reluctant to subject their child to a sur­
gical or interventional procedure, especially when the aneu­
rysm has been identified incidentally. Although this reluctance 
is understandable, the literature on the natural history of pedi­
atric aneurysms suggests that these lesions evolve and grow, 
and new aneurysm formation is a common phenomenon. Thus 
we rarely recommend conservative management, except in 
select cases such as mycotic aneurysms; instead, we recom­
mend that most pediatric aneurysms be aggressively treated 
with microsurgery, endovascular techniques, or a combination 
of the two.

aneurysms, 75% of which occurred in children. It is estimated 
that 14% to 39% of all pediatric intracranial aneurysms may be 
due to trauma.12 Similarly, up to 10% of pediatric intracranial 
aneurysms are thought to be of mycotic in origin, frequently 
secondary to endocarditis.13,14 Mycotic aneurysms are frequently 
distal in the vascular tree and involve the middle cerebral artery 
(MCA) branches. The most common organisms are Staphylococcus 
aureus and Streptococcus species,13 but cases involving Aspergillus, 
Candida, and Phycomycetes species and cases associated with bone 
marrow transplantation and human immunodeficiency virus have 
also been reported.14 However, caution must be exercised with 
regard to the literature on traumatic and mycotic aneurysms in 
the pediatric population because the sample size in many of these 
reports is too small for definitive conclusions to be drawn.
Fusiform and dissecting aneurysms account for 60% of 
pediatric aneurysms but less than 1% of adult aneurysms.15 These 
aneurysms may be caused by spontaneous dissections caused by 
connective tissue disorders or trauma, or they may be iatrogenic.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF PEDIATRIC ANEURYSMS
The exact etiology of pediatric aneurysms is not well known and 
is a matter of great controversy. Children are rarely exposed 
to the factors that are thought to cause aneurysm formation 
in adults; the likely mechanism of aneurysm formation among 
adults is chronic stress due to hypertension and inflammation, 
which are probably caused by smoking and other comorbidities. 
This lack of exposure in children has led some investigators to 
postulate that pediatric aneurysms may be congenital.6 However, 
a large autopsy series in children did not detect any incidental 
aneurysms,7 casting doubt on a congenital etiology. Lasjaunias 
and colleagues8 have proposed that structural defects, which 
likely arise from genetic alterations, cause pediatric aneurysms. 
What is certain is that the etiology of these pediatric lesions is 
different from that of adult saccular aneurysms.
Lending support to the belief that a genetic structural defect 
is a cause for pediatric aneurysms, several reports have noted 
an increased incidence of aneurysms in patients with aortic 
coarctation, autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, 
fibromuscular dysplasia, or connective tissue disorder; therefore 
close follow-up of these patients with screening magnetic 
resonance angiography (MRA) is warranted (Box 248.1).6,9,10

Risk factors for development of intracranial aneurysms 
include factors such as polycystic kidney disease; smoking; 
hypertension; aortic coarctation; α1-antitrypsin deficiency 
(115); connective tissue diseases, for example, Ehlers–Danlos 
syndrome Type IV (100–102, 116–118); fibromuscular dys-

Some families have been identified with a genetically 
heterogeneous pattern of inheritance of intracranial aneu-
rysms. Within this group of patients, most will have only 
one other affected family member, usually a sibling (121). 
Screening of asymptomatic patients with polycystic kidney 
disease detects an aneurysm prevalence of approximately 
12%, but the prevalence increases to 25% when there is also 
a family history of intracranial aneurysms (122,123).
Among all patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hem-
